That is a decision on the Prosecution's motion to hear the testimony of Witness 41 - that's the witness who will testify today - via video-conference link. On the 2nd of October, 2008, the Prosecution filed a motion requesting, among other matters, to hear the testimony of Witness 41 via video-conference link from Croatia on the 16th of October, 2008. On the 6th and the 7th October 2008 respectively all three Defence teams stated that they did not object to the Prosecution's request. On the 7th October 2008, having received at least an informal indication of the Defence positions at that time, the Chamber decided to grant the request for a video-conference link and informed the parties accordingly through an informal communication. According to Rule 81 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a chamber may order that proceedings be conducted by way of a video-conference link if it is consistent with the interests of justice. The test of Rule 81 bis is met if the witness is unable to come to the Tribunal, if the testimony of the witness is sufficiently important to make it unfair to the requesting party to proceed without it, and if the accused is not prejudiced in the exercise of his or her rights to confront the witness. The Chamber has taken into consideration the highly advanced age of Witness 41, who is in his 80s, and his physical condition. Both Witness 41's son and an investigator of the Prosecution who visited Witness 41 several times have expressed serious concerns that, in view of his age, Witness 41 is not in a condition to travel to The Hague to testify. The Chamber is therefore satisfied that the advanced age of Witness 41 makes him unable to travel to the Tribunal to testify. The witness is expected to testify, inter alia, about scheduled killing incident number 8, the shelling of his village, and the looting and burning of houses in his village, as alleged in the indictment. The Chamber is satisfied that his prospective testimony is sufficiently important to make it unfair to the Prosecution to proceed without it. Finally, the Defence has not argued, and the Chamber does not find that the accused would be prejudiced in the exercise of their right to confront the witness. Consequently, the Chamber finds that it is consistent with the interests of justice to grant the Prosecution's request to hear Witness 41's testimony via video-conference link and the Prosecution's motion is therefore granted. That same evening he found the bodies of Uros Ognjenovic and Uros Saric who appeared to have been killed in Uros Ognjenovic's yard. The bodies remained in the same position for days before they were collected. Mr. Ognjenovic could not find any police available to investigate the killings. Mr. Ognjenovic left Kakanj on the 26th of August 1995 and left the Krajina on the 15th September 1995 in a convoy. He returned to Kakanj in 1997. utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, in your statement from 23rd and 24th January, 1999, which is P989, I believe, now, that's tab 1 in B/C/S, Madam Registrar. On page 2 in B/C/S and in English for e-court you mentioned that the civilian population of Kakanj started leaving after they heard the shelling of Knin. Could you tell us in more detail, why did they leave?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They were leaving because they were -- they believed that they would be coming over, that shells would be landing on the village. I don't know how it came to the point that it was said that they should flee to the hills out of the villages. I myself decided to stay behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Why did you stay, Mr. Ognjenovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed behind, listening to the radio, where it was said whoever was not guilty need not leave. I was listening to Tudjman's statement that was heard over the radio every hour. My wife was in the hospital. I thought that she had died and I was supposed to go to Knin that morning. As the -- as Storm started, I stayed home. I decided that I should best stay where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: How many people of the people who stayed in the village, if anyone, were part of the -- of the army?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: None of them did. Three women stayed behind and six elderly people. Out of the six, one girl, she wasn't young, she was a spinster, was killed and the three who were killed, Vojin Saric and the other Saric who -- Uros, who was -- they were brothers. One of them was born in 1920 and the other in 1911. They were elderly people, a bit out of their wits, and they were both killed. Uros Ognjenovic was also killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ognjenovic, on page 4 of the same statement, you mentioned two soldiers who came to you in the village on the 8th of August, 1995. What, if anything, did they say to you, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They told me, one of them asked me why I had stayed behind, I would have done better to have left with the others. He said, I won't be touching anyone but all sorts of -- all manner of things will happen. I cannot vouch for you. Don't stray away from your homes. Stay in your homes. Well, but I ended up being killed, or rather, wounded in my own backyard.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: To be clear, Mr. Ognjenovic, your wounding did not happen on that same day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Come again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: As you stated in your statement previously, the wounding that you mention in your statement, when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th, on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: When the two were killed and I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now you mentioned also that soldiers came to your house on the 9th of August, the following day, and burned your house. Can you describe the exchange -- in more detail the exchange between you on that date.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: You mean with them?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: With the ones who came over to set fire? One of them had a rifle trained at me and I said, What is that rifle for? I'm not putting up any resistance. Put it away or else you will kill me, I will not be killing anyone, it's a disgrace, really, you were offending us and you were saying all of you Serbs have to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If I can now turn to the events of the 18th of August, 1995. This is page 6 in B/C/S; and page 7 in English, for e-court and for Madam Registrar. You said that you were having dinner with other villagers, and you heard a sound of some people walking to your house. Could you describe what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They were shouting, Where are those nine people? There was somebody who said that there were nine of us there. They were shouting, Where are the nine people? Come out. Radoslav, and I did come out and he trained his rifle at me. I don't know what happened next. I don't know what hit me, what he hit me with. I got in a coma and I was out, like dead for a couple of hours. And I don't know what happened next until I finally came to. I woke out of the coma, how shall I put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What were the two men who approached you wearing, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: You mean soldiers? Well, they had the military gear, uniform, rifles. I don't know. That was secondary, in my view. I couldn't see any of that. All of it took place in the space of ten seconds. They got into the yard and ... I don't know what they hit me with. I had my skin burst here, I had a cut, and it was swollen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you remember what, if anything, they had on their heads?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: What a soldier normally wears. Those caps. I don't know what they are. It was of secondary importance to me, as I said. The only thing I know was that he was shouting furiously through gritted teeth before even entering our yard, Come out so that I can kill you all. I didn't think I was going to survive.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, how far is your house from house of Uros Ognjenovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Around 200 metres. 200 to 250.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know who, if anyone, from the Croatian authorities approached you in relation to these deaths?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody did. Those that were passing by asked me, Who hit you? I said, A soldier did. I had my head bandaged so he could see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: At any point after these killings occurred and today, Mr. Ognjenovic, did anyone approach you in relation to these killings? From the Croatian police or other investigative authorities.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody did. Nobody did. Six days after the two men were killed, I was almost alone. Almost alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, if we could show what was 65 ter 5970 and has now been assigned a P number, P996, be shown on screen. That's tab 17 and 18, Madam Registrar, page 04651409. That's page 7 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And if I could just read a paragraph on page 7 to you. This is a record of exhumation conducted on the 17th of April, 2000 on behalf of the county Court in Sibenik in the Zadar town cemetery and it says: "Present during the exhumation were Cedo Ognjenovic from Kakanj. Personal identification number 2012930382111, brother of Uros Ognjenovic; and Mirko Ognjenovic from Kakanj, personal identification number 1611921382106, brother-in-law of Uros Ognjenovic. Would you be able to con --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now do you remember identifying Uros Ognjenovic as is stated in this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, this document mentions on the same page that the bodies exhumed under the numbers 445 and 446 which were later identified as Uros Saric and Uros Ognjenovic wore military green pants. Why, to your knowledge, would these two men have worn such clothing?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Uros Saric had such trousers because his son was on the police force. He gave him a pair of police trousers that he no longer had any use for. He gave that pair of trousers to his father. That was not true, that they had military trousers on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: How old were these two men when they were killed, Mr. Ognjenovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Uros Saric was born in 1920, so he was 75; and Uros Ognjenovic was born in 1928.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time for Mr. Ognjenovic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Frolich. Mr. Ognjenovic, Mr. Misetic will now put questions to you. Mr. Misetic is Defence counsel for Mr. Gotovina. You will see him now on your screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you speak to -- do you recall speaking to the Office of the Prosecutor within the past week regarding your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall telling the Office of the Prosecutor that -- when you were asked why people left the village of Kakanj, did you tell the Office of the Prosecutor that: "They left because villages were being shelled and also because people were told to leave by the local committee and that fuel would be distributed but that it was not."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what was this local committee? Who was in the committee ...

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: How should I know? A couple of people who were there who were not in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And were they from your village?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Saric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who else was there. I know that Dragan was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you speak to Dragan on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't even see him. I didn't even see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How did you hear that Dragan Saric told people to leave and said that fuel would be distributed?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't say that; others were saying that. A drum of fuel was found in his home and the army that got there took it away in the evening. Others were then saying that it had been brought over there in order to be distributed to the villagers. I don't know if this was indeed the case. This is how it was talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me a little bit about the army arriving in the evening. When -- you mean the RSK army?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. No, well, they came on a tank. There was a tank going ahead of them. They were singing and they immediately set two or three houses on fire, and in the beginning when they arrived they drank, there was wine flowing and they sang and drank until midnight. So they set the barn -- the -- the barn, Dragan's barn on fire immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just -- I think the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think everyone noticed that there may be a matter which we should further --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- specify, that's clear. Ms. Frolich, please proceed -- Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, I'm actually talking to you about your statement that -- actually you told the Office of the Prosecutor that people were told by the local committee that fuel would be distributed but it was not. And now you say that there was a drum of fuel at Dragan Saric's home and that the army, when it got there, took it away in the evening. Which army took the drum of fuel?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian army, those people who came to the village first. They didn't take the drum. They actually poured it out and they lit -- and they set the house on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know why the fuel couldn't have been used the day before by the villagers who were fleeing the village on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Because they didn't know. No one knew of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, when Dragan Saric and these other people told the villagers to leave and that fuel would be distributed, are you saying that -- that Dragan Saric then never distributed the fuel to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, no one even knew about this. It was only later that there were conjectures that fuel was actually distributed. But whether it was or not, I don't know. The only thing I know is that there was a barrel of fool in the house, or actually it was in the garage. Whether it belonged to him or not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Djevrska is a town that's -- that neighbours your town. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the army of the Republika Serbian Krajina was using private houses and some warehouses in Djevrska for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, this was a cooperative building, the building that was used by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And how far is Djevrska, approximately, in kilometres from your village?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell by the direction and sound of the shelling on the 4th whether the shells that were coming from Sibenik were in fact landing in Djevrska?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the witness could be asked whether he actually observed any shells falling in Djevrska instead of by direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the answer -- in view of the question the answer is not unambiguous, Mr. Misetic, could you tell whether. Is the answer yes, I can tell; or is the answer yes, they came; or they landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did shells, to your knowledge, land in Djevrska on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for sure. But I did not see this. I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, there are villages -- Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask who else is in the room with the witness right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we be informed, Ms. Alvarez, who is in the room, apart from the technician, you, and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was no one else. I'm informed by the registrar here in The Hague that he had a telephone conversation about channels, English channel, which caused some problems over there and that is -- so therefore what we saw and heard is for 99.9 per cent certain is the conversation between --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- representatives of the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. I even -- the last answer, if I hear something, it could also mean several things. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you said, Mr. Ognjenovic, that you heard it, meaning when I asked you did shells, to your knowledge, land in Djevrska on the 4th of August, you said yes, for sure, but I did not see this. I heard it. What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I heard the shells falling and I was also told by the person who was directing the fire, he said, I shelled so-and-so's house and I told him, You shouldn't have done it, and later on, when he went hunting, he told me how he was the one, the man who directed the fire, who shelled this particular house and destroyed it. I think that the army was in there. It was a big building but there was no one. There was no military personnel there. It was just a private home but it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is this a home in Djevrska that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Djevrska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In villages -- there are villages that neighbour your village, like Smrdelje [phoen], Varivode, Bratiskovci, Plastovo, Rupa, Laskovici. In any of those villages during or prior to Operation Storm was there a presence of the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, when -- you mentioned when you were being asked some questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. His answer did not get translated into English. At least verbally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But it appears -- it appears on the screen as being translated into English, but I might have heard the original answer which was yes there, I think. And that would mean, yes, this sufficiently corrects the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I see it on the screen, I just didn't hear it in the headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there is no dispute about what the witness said. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in answer to a question by Ms. Frolich that you thought that the shelling seemed to be on the corridor for refugees. Do you recall saying that this morning?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did the -- did the corridor pass near your village?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't. It was a bit farther away. Farther away. Some eight to ten kilometres away, shells fell there the whole day, the next day, throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you where the shells landed. What I'm asking you is you know there was a corridor through which people left the so-called Krajina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard later on that this was the way they went, and from my house you could see the shells landing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This corridor -- I'm asking now about the corridor and not about where the shells landed. How close was the corridor to your village?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: About ten kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina, as it was withdrawing, would have passed through or near your village on the evening of the 4th or the morning of the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did pass. They, too, did not know where they were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you see these soldiers pass?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How many soldiers did you see pass?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I saw some of them, but I know that they passed there in trucks because I was a bit away from the main road, so I couldn't really see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you hear tanks?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. There were no tanks in the Serbian army. They didn't have them in our parts, in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have two documents that I'd like to show here in Court. I don't have them for the witness but I'm going to ask him a few questions on the basis of what is contained in the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have -- are they uploaded in e-court for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's see how to proceed. Let's first have a look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. First, Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 4765 on the screen, please. And page -- and it -- I'm sorry, it has a P number. It's P784; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then most likely it will be over there as well. No, it's P -- it's an old number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's an old number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... assigned today, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, I'm going to read to you from two documents and then ask you a couple of questions on it. The first is a report from United Nations Civilian Police that visited Kakanj on the 28th of August, 1995 and found that most of the houses in Kakanj were intact and that they did not see any people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could go to 65 ter 2133, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a report that we have here in court, Mr. Ognjenovic. It from is the United Nations Military Observers, dated 27 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, Mr. Registrar. Third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, I'm just going to read to you, this is a report that was filed by some members of the United Nations that visited with you, and here's what they wrote. They said: "On 21 August 1995 at 1135 in the morning, Valery Rublik and Dimitri Batiochenkov found two dead bodies in Kakanj in the courtyard of house number 45. It was stated by a resident, Ognjenovic Mirko, aged 74, to the UNMOs that two HV soldiers came to the village at 1800 on 18 August 1995."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Beat him and killed these two people." And then a sentence below it says that you -- it says: "This man also stated that two other Serbs had burnt his house at 1530 on 16 August 1995." Now, my question is: Do you recall telling members of the United Nations that your house had been burned by two other Serbs and giving them a specific date and time as to when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No. It didn't happen that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now that I've read this back to you, does it refresh your recollection that, in fact, your house was burned on the 16th of August at 1530 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was not on the 16th; it was on the 8th when his house was set on fire, on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall telling --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The 8th or the 9th, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall telling these UN Military Observers that two Serbs had burnt your house down?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm sure I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: This question was already asked before. I just wanted to put that on the record, and the witness answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think he is answered it, Your Honour. I'm just going to tender the exhibit now anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you just told us that this was -- was it this one that was already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, it was the previous one. That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this one needs a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D872.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D872 is admitted into evidence. Now, about question asked, question answered, the earlier question was -- contained several elements, date, persons, and if you get a confirmation that it went in a different way, it could be about the date, about perpetrators so to that extent there was a good reason to further explore that matter, Ms. Frolich. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ognjenovic, is it true to say that when the Croatian army passed through Kakanj the first time, that Croatian soldiers did not harm anyone?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it true --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't even see anyone. They didn't see any civilians or any military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that when the Croatian army passed through Kakanj for the first time on the 5th of August that they did not search any houses?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't. They only set three or four houses on fire, right away, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, is it possible that you're mistaken and that in fact the Croatian army only set one haystack on fire, maybe just in order to signal the place where they had reached?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for sure they set on fire the hay and the house, right at the beginning of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, this again is a composite question, what was done and for what purpose, and I would like you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll break it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have a young academic before you, that might be different. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask it a different way, Mr. Ognjenovic. Is it possible that you're mistaken and that instead of burning houses on the 5th of August, the only thing that was burned by the Croatian army on the 5th of August was a single haystack?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: There were more than one but they set on fire at the very -- on the very edge of the village, they set on fire a house and some hay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, do you know if Croatian police units were established in the neighbouring village of Bratiskovci two or three days after the end of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so but I did not see them. I was not -- I didn't go to Bratiskovci but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, in your statement, at page 5 of your 1999 statement you said to the Prosecution that on three or four occasions - and this is now at the fourth full paragraph: "On three or four occasions police in blue uniforms came to the village. On these uniform the was the word policija on the sleeves. I think they were --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And they brought for us, and this is what I said, that's how it happened. This was later on on the 6th or the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were about to say that they brought you something. What did they bring you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They brought bread for us, salami, stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement you think they were the civilian police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, but they did not say who they were, whether they were the civilian police or the military police. I think they were the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You also say in your statement: "When the police were in the village, the soldiers did not come stealing and looting." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't. There was no looting. This happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever come to any understanding at that time as to why people you believed to be soldiers weren't looting when the police was in the village?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why. I guess they didn't let them, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President -- or, Mr. Registrar, I -- keeping in mind the procedure that we have in place about confronting witnesses with other statements of other witnesses I have taken him through and put to him the matters in the statement and now I'd like to confront him with the statement of another witness and ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, not having --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not knowing what witness statement you're talking about I can't verify, but you announce that in your view you've covered --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the substance of other witness statement without putting it to the witness and that you're now moving to put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have hard copy for the Bench because we didn't it uploaded it into e-court since we won't be tendering the statement into evidence. This is the statement of Rajko Gajica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, you know who Rajko Gajica is. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And he was a villager with you during the month of August 1995. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me just tell you what Mr. Gajica told the Office of the Prosecutor. This is on page 2 of his statement, second paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he said, but Rajko was the one who washed my wound out and dressed it, and then he went to Bratiskovci looking for protection and he was taken away to Sibenik. On the next day, he was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, Mr. Misetic will tell you about the statement given by Mr. Gajica. But before he does so, could you tell us what you said when you said, On the next day, he was ... That was the next day after he was taken away to Sibenik. Could you tell us what you then said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He went to Bratiskovci. I think the police was down there and he went there seeking protection. They said they could not -- we cannot protect you but we can take to you Sibenik, and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just let me ask you one additional question before I go into this statement. Mr. Ognjenovic, do you recall telling Mr. Gajica when you came to his house on the evening of the 18th after you had been struck by these two individuals, did you tell him that it was two people who did this to you, one of whom was a soldier, and that the other one was in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was not in civilian clothes. I didn't say that, nor was he in civilian clothes. Both of them were in military clothes. I came to Rajko's as wounded as I was and he said that he heard them walk past because they were on foot. He also said that he had heard shooting over at our place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for the Court's reference, I won't put it to him specifically, but it's page 3, second paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me also read a portion of Mr. Gajica's statement to you. Mr. Gajica told the Office of the Prosecutor on page 2, second paragraph from the bottom, that: "On the 5th of August, 1995, about six -- at about 6.00 to 7.00 p.m., the regular Croatian army soldiers entered Kakanj. On that day, the Croatian soldiers did not harm anybody. They have just set a haystack on fire in the end of the village, maybe just in order to signal the place which they reached. The military column moving on foot and by trucks passed through Kakanj and four more villages. On that evening, the soldiers did not search the houses, were not threatening the villages." Now, Mr. Ognjenovic, is it in fact true that when the Croatian army arrived on the 5th of August that they did not harm -- let me -- that they did not set any houses on fire and in fact were just passing through the village?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: But they did. They set both the house and the haystack on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this might be a good time for a break, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us an indication on how much time would you need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would hope I will be done within half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ognjenovic, we'll take a break and we'll resume at 11.00, and I'm quite confident that we'll finish this morning. We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, we'll continue. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, referring to page 5 of your 1999 statement, you said that on most of the times when they were looting, they were in civilian cars. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. There were both women and men who looted everything they could find.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turning to the death of Danica Saric. Now, when you -- it's correct that you assisted in removing the body from the well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you did not check to see if there were there any wounds or injuries on the body. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you some questions about --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: There was nothing. We assumed that it was she herself who threw herself there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain for the Court why you assumed that she threw herself into the well?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. She was fearful of everything, being as she was a spinster, a virgin, and she must have been afraid that the army would have man-handled her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I please have 1D00-0450. Madam Registrar in Zagreb, this is tab 3. I don't think it's necessary that the witness review it, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, do you recall speaking to members of the Croatian police roughly in May of 2004, where you talked to the police about the death of Danica Saric?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Some persons did come, but I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember speaking to any police officers about the death of Danica Saric?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can scroll down on this document, please, last paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall -- is it true when the deceased Uros Ognjenovic and Rajko Gajica changed her clothes for the burial they didn't see -- notice any type of wounds or injuries while on her -- injuries on her body while dressing her?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: There was nothing. There were none. But we didn't change her clothes. We weren't able to. She was all bloated from being in the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall perhaps telling anyone from the Croatian police that Danica was very scared of the military police Operation Storm. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you know if -- or do you recall ever telling the police that Danica suffered from a mild nervous illness?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is that a true statement, that she suffered from a mild nervous illness?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall her ever saying, It would be better if they killed me than them doing something to me?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall telling the police that you didn't see any armed soldiers or civilians prior to her death and that they -- they only started to arrive in Kakanj after the death -- the fatal wounding of Danica Saric?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: -- remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it, to the best of your recollection, true that you didn't see any armed soldiers or civilians in Kakanj until after the death of Danica Saric?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, I didn't. But for the two men I referred to earlier on who told me that I would have done better had I left, too, because all manner of things would happen. Except for the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender into evidence 1D00-0450.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- there are no objections. May I take it it is not tendered under Rule 92 ter but just as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: An exhibit, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number D873.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D873 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Ognjenovic, prior to her death if Danica ever told anyone that she was going to drown herself?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: She didn't tell anyone. She said that she was very frightened, easily scared, and that she didn't know what would become of her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D00-0454, please, I'm just going to read an excerpt of this, and there's no need to show it to the witness in Zagreb. And the rest of the documents, Your Honour, I will bar table as they are part of a broader -- the broader file on this incident that we've obtained, some of which was put in by the Prosecution on direct. If we could go to page 3 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is an Official Note taken in 2004 of Rajko Gajica. And in the third paragraph it says, towards -- towards the middle: "Danica got scared and said to Uros Saric, 'here they come, they're burning across the village, I'm going to throw myself in the well.' The day before, Danica and Uros Saric were harassed by uniformed persons unfamiliar to them and Danica was probably scared because of that and told him she was going to drown herself. He tried to persuade her not and Danica left to his tavern afterwards." Now, did Uros Saric perhaps ever tell you that Danica told him that she was scared and she was going to drown herself in the well? Mr. Ognjenovic, I don't know if you heard me. My question was: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Uros did say that. Uros did say that, that she had told him, that Danica had told him that she didn't know what to do, that she was scared and that she would ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That she would what, Mr. Ognjenovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You said that Uros said that she said -- that she told him that she didn't know what to do and that she was scared and that she would ... and then we didn't get the rest of the sentence. What did you say that Danica told --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: She didn't say that she was going to drown herself but that she didn't know what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender the entire document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D874, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D874 is admitted into evidence. Again, this is a -- this is also an Official Note --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it is not a statement taken for the purpose of these proceedings. Therefore it is not a 92 ter admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ognjenovic, do you recall being interviewed by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who talked to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. And if we could now in D784, go to page 6 of, please, of that document. D874, I'm sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the events that took place on the 18th of August, 1995, do you recall being interviewed by a Croatian police officer on the 16th of May, 2000?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could now go to page 9 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you recall in July 2000 that the police conducted an interview with you and Radoslav Ognjenovic and that you were shown a series of pictures to see if you could identify anyone who may have been involved in the incident on the 18th of August, 1995? Do you remember being shown pictures of people who may have done this to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall whether you were able to pick anyone out of those photos as the person who was involved in the incident on the 18th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't say that we knew anyone. There was an individual by the name of Mladen. When he trained the rifle at me, the other one shouted, No, Mladjo, do not shoot. And then a police officer brought a photograph number 9, an individual by the name of Mladen was under number 9 but I had no idea who that person was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you say Mladen, could it have been Nedjelko and not Mladen as the name?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Nedjelko, right, Nedjelko, yes, yes. I confused it to -- yes, Nedjelko; Nedjo, do not shoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this incident took place on the 18th of August. Do you -- just one second. Now, you say in your statement at page 8 that Radoslav told you that Rajko Gajica had gone to Bratiskovci to find the police and report about the dead bodies. Do you know if in fact Rajko Gajica the next day went to --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the very next day this incident was reported to the civilian police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could have on the screen, please, P992. It's the first paragraph in the English, if we could scroll down, please. If we could go to the next page, please, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In this -- there was a complaint filed on the 28th of August, 1995 by the son of Uros Saric. And in the complaint, he writes, six lines in, in the English version: "As far as I am aware -- " no, I'm sorry. Five lines down. He writes in his complaint that: "Uros Saric and Uros Ognjenovic were killed. Radoslav Ognjenovic and Mirko Ognjenovic were injured by three persons, two of whom were uniformed. Do you know, is it possible, Mr. Ognjenovic, that this incident involved not two individuals but three individuals, one of whom was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No. Only Uros was in civilian clothes. Nobody else, of those who came over to my place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Mr. Ognjenovic, thank you very much for answering my questions. I do have two bar table submissions to make, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be if we followed the same procedure --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you read out their numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that Mr. Registrar will assign exhibit numbers to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This would be -- actually I think it's three bar table submissions. 1D00-0454, this is from the police file on the murders of -- it's in already. I'm sorry. That is in as D874. So 1D00-0445, this is a Republic of Croatia MUP criminal report regarding the murder of Vojin Saric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number D875.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Next is a record of exhumation of Danica Saric, the women in the well, and it is 1D00-0441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D876, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection? Yes, no, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Sorry, no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the last one is 1D00-0472, it is a Republic of Croatia MUP special report on the murders in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I believe this is one of the documents included in our bar table submission, if I'm not mistaken. Therefore if that can be double-checked. We have no objection, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's check.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If Ms. Frolich can tell us which P number it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Just a moment. I believe that is 65 ter 5300 which became P1003. I believe we are talking about the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have one page as P1003. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 5300 became P1003, special report from the Zadar-Knin police administration to the office of the military prosecutor, Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My submission, Your Honour, has seven pages total out of the file. So the cover -- the first pages is -- may be identical. The rest, I think we have additional pages in our submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Well, what we received from you is also one page and that is the cover page. I'm not sure what other documents you would be referring to. Maybe they are under other Defence numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, I think ... we'll look in e-court right now and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1003 is indeed a one-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And our submission in e-court, Your Honour, is seven pages long. So it may be a printing error on ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I apologise. If this exhibit also includes the document from the 20th February 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And the criminal report record on the 28th August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: These two documents I believe are also part of our bar table submission, Mr. President, these two documents, and they are -- they are P1002 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the 20th of February, 1996 document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes. And P992 respectfully, Mr. President, the complaint from 28th of August 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would in total make the same number of pages as Mr. Misetic was tendering? Could we -- could the parties just verify during the next break whether there's anything new in what Mr. Misetic wants to tender. It's from the bar table anyhow, so therefore -- which would mean -- is this -- was this the last one, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that no number has yet been assigned to this. We'll leave that for -- until after the break. D875 and D876 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions. I'm looking at the other Defence teamS. Mr. Kay, no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Ms. Frolich, is there any need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Just two brief questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ognjenovic, Ms. Frolich will put some further questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, earlier when asked about setting haystacks, army setting haystacks on fire, you mentioned that there was also a house set on fire on the 5th of August, 1995. That's page 32, line 15.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And can you tell us whose house was this that was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: It was the house of Nikola Ognjenovic and Marko Ognjenovic, two houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that two houses were in fact set on fire on that day, Mr. Ognjenovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And who were these two persons that you just named?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, who were they? Nikola Ognjenovic and Marko Ognjenovic's houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What was their occupation; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the house owners?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Were these people civilians or were they members of the army, Mr. Ognjenovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Were they present in the village or were they gone at the time that their houses were set on fire?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They had left.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now another question is when you spoke about a person directing fire, shelling fire, on page 26, line 23 of the transcript you said: "I heard the shelling falling and I was also told by the person who was directing the fire, he said, I shelled so-and-so's house and I told him, You shouldn't have done it, and later on, when he went hunting he told me how he was the one, the man who directed the fire who shelled this particular house and destroyed it."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: When was this, Mr. Ognjenovic? When?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: When the shelling was?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No. When were you told by this person?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, a year later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And who was this person?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: He was Pulic, I can't recall his first name. I know his father's name is Jure, so he was Jure Pulic's son. He told me. He said that he was the one who directed or guided the fire and he figured that there were troops in the house so he directed the fire, the shells to shell that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What was his nationality? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The man who was guiding the fire? A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, I might have a few questions for you. You told us about the Croatian army coming into the village. I think that was on the 5th of August, where you said that two houses and a haystack had been put on fire. Now, how --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell me, the army, Croatian army coming in the village, could you give me an indication as to how many approximately were there? And I'm --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: That, I wouldn't know. I don't know how many there were. I only heard about it. I was in hiding in the plumb orchard next to my house. I only heard the noise, their voices and their song, because they were singing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you seen any vehicles they were using?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anything. I could only hear a tank leading and then there were people coming after the tank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were on foot or ...

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They were on trucks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were on trucks.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They were driving slowly through the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you observed that yourself; you did see these trucks?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But it was dark, it was night-time, so I could hear them coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you gain any impression about how many approximately were there, how many of these trucks?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I have no idea how many there were nor what went on. There were two stores in the village, shops. They were open. The doors had been broken down. That was the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would now like to move to what is in your statement about what happened on the 8th of August; that is, where you said two soldiers came up to you. They asked you where you were going. You said, I'm going to feed my pigs. You remember these soldiers who told you that they did not wish to harm you in any way but that others might come who would not be that kind. Now, when these two soldiers came to you --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said to me ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what I'd like to know is, when these two soldiers came to you, were they the only soldiers in the village, were they part of a larger company, or were these just two individual soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: There were two soldiers. There were only two soldiers. They asked for my car keys. I said I didn't have them. Then they asked, What are you doing? And I said, I'm feeding my pigs. And they said, Well, leave those pigs alone and look after yourself. That's what they said to me. Because you can expect anything to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So at that moment you did not observe any other soldiers around in your village. You just saw the two.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Only those two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember how they came. Were they in a car or were they on foot?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They came by car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of car that was? Was that a military vehicle, was that a civilian vehicle, was it ...

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't really know. I can't remember what their plates were, nor anything else. I didn't -- I wasn't even looking at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you did see that car?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They got out of the car and came up to me. Yes, I did see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour of that car?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, similar questions for what happened on the 9th of August, the day after that. That is the event where you said the soldiers shot your dog. Let's start with the beginning. You said in your statement: "I heard a vehicle stop nearby." Did these soldiers come in that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. They came in their own vehicle. It was a military vehicle. And he shot the dog which was standing next to my leg. And then they left. They were setting my house on fire and the other one was pointing his gun at me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And they came in a military vehicle. You have observed that vehicle yourself.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean observe? I wasn't observing. I was in the yard. They left their car outside and he set my house on fire, my stable, the haystacks, everything. And then I rushed because I wanted to take the cultivator, the motor cultivator out of the garage, and they said, Come on, move on because you will get killed. And that's what he said, so I took it and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I asked you whether you observed the vehicle, I wanted to know whether you saw with your own eyes this vehicle to be a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a military vehicle, because it was grey, so it's sure that it was a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, at that point in time, when your house was set on fire, did you see any other military people or military vehicles apart from the ones who came to you in the village?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Because my house was at the end of the village. I was at the end of the village. And they set about ten houses on fire on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us, what's the total number of houses in your village?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about 100 or so, I think. This was a small hamlet. It wasn't a real village, just a hamlet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, now, in total, so during these days both on the 5th and the 9th, how many houses finally ended up to be burned? You told us ten on the 9th; two on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Then it was ten houses. Later on, they set other houses on fire. As far as I'm concerned, in fact, there weren't -- there were only ten houses that were set on fire then. But later on, more of them were set on fire, about half of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does this mean that at the end half of the village was burned, houses were burned?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also told us in your statement that: "The soldiers came to the village most days and they were looting anything they could find from the houses." Were these -- and you were talking about first --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they come as individuals, one or two, perhaps three, or did they come in groups of more persons?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They came in ones and twos, two or three, and they carried stuff away, each for their own -- for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If they were carrying stuff away, as you told us, what kind of vehicles were they using?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Civilian vehicles. Most of them were civilian vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers, Mr. Ognjenovic. We'll see whether there are further questions for you. Mr. Misetic may have one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, I just wanted to clarify something that may not have appeared on the transcript. You said that ten houses were burned and then after you left you learned that more houses had been burned. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So outside of these ten houses you didn't actually -- you weren't actually there in the village when any other houses other than these ten were burned. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't there. I was in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Ognjenovic, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming to Zagreb and for answering all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I hope that you will arrive safely home again today, and it will be soon your birthday. I wish you health --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for the future. We --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can -- we can conclude the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are a few procedural issues left. I'd like to briefly deal with them. First is the Chamber has considered the request for a videolink for Witness 17, which is, I think, next week -- no, not next week but the Wednesday when we return after the recess. Is that ... 29th?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided that it will grant the videolink. There were no objections and the reasons will follow in the usual way in oral decision. Next issue I'd like to raise is the agreement that has been reached by the parties on the -- on the map issue, what are administrative borders how was it before Operation Storm, how was it after Operation Storm. In our first -- in the first report, in an e-mail sent to the Chamber, reference was made to maps which are in the binder of maps the Chamber has been provided with but which are not in evidence. So, therefore, that e-mail, the text of that e-mail without these maps being in evidence might not resolve the matter entirely but we have meanwhile received another e-mail in which a map is apparently attached. I have not yet looked at that map. Everyone may be aware that I have some allergies for some kind type of maps that is projected maps or -- we'll have a look at that map. What the Chamber would like to have everything clear on the record which might be best done by a filing, perhaps a joint filing with the parties in which they set out the agreement with an attached map, if the Chamber would have difficulties with the map, again I have not looked at it yet, we will let you know, but otherwise the parties are invited to prepare a joint filing in which the matters they agreed upon are set out and the map being attached. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just for clarification, the map that we e-mailed around last night, actually that Mr. Margetts e-mailed around last night is a map that is not part of the binder of maps that you were looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. The previous e-mails made reference to maps who are in that binder of maps. The new one is attached and I did understand that that's a different map. But I just have not yet looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just want to be sure that all the parties understand the map that you are looking for, what we did was -- I should say the Prosecution created a map of the municipalities that are the subject of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and what it is called in the e-mail, Croatian municipalities, 1992, and then, underscore, new indictment area, jpg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I open it for a second and see that it needs. Yes. That is ... Yes, it is a map with -- at the top it reads case IT-06-90-PT, Gotovina, et al, indictment, municipalities and then a legend, settlement according to the 1991 census and it distinguishes between indictment municipalities in grey and other municipalities in white. That's the map --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is the map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you're referring to. Perhaps that could be -- I think the easier way to do it is to set out the agreement, including temporal aspects, and then attach the map and have this filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have a -- there's another matter in relation with the last witness. The Prosecution has filed a report on the 19th of May of this year on protective measures for witnesses -- Witness 11 and Witness 42. The reason why the 92 quater statement of Witness 42 was protected was because we did not know what to expect in relation to Witness 41. Now this is clear, meanwhile. Therefore, I would like to hear from the Prosecution whether there is any further objection against the evidence of Witness 42 to become public.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the statement of Witness 42, which was admitted pursuant to Rule 92 quater, will be a public document. It is the document that was admitted by a decision on admission of two witnesses, pursuant to Rule 92 quater, which was 24th of April, 2008, and you'll find that in paragraph 10. So it's not a decision on the witness -- on Witness 42, it's just about the statement of Witness 42, which will from now on be a public document. Then I have a few decision to deliver. First decision being a decision on the admission of D717, which is currently MFIed. On the 25th of July during the cross-examination of Witness Roland Dangerfield, at transcript page 7285 and 7286, the Defence presented the witness with an article published in the Croatian press in February 2007 which contained an interview with the then Russian ambassador to Croatia. The interview was marked for identification as D717. In the interview, the ambassador made reference to the Z-4 plan and the reaction of the authorities in Knin to this plan. The Defence sought to admit this article into evidence, submitting that it is relevant because it refers to the peace negotiations between Krajina officials and representatives of the Croatian government and Mr. Akashi's visit to Knin, both related to the Z-4 plan. The Prosecution objected to the admission of this article, submitting that the Defence had failed to lay the proper foundation for its admission, as the witness was unable to comment on the article. Only a portion of this article, the original of which is in B/C/S, has been translated into English. It is on the basis of this partial translation that the Chamber has decided upon the admission of D717. D717 contains information about the presentation of the Z-4 plan to Milan Martic and his refusal to receive the plan. Neither the existence of the Z-4 plan nor Martic's reaction to this plan seems to be a contested issue in this case. D717 does not contradict evidence that the Chamber has already heard from other witnesses concerning this plan, including Peter Galbraith, whose name is mentioned in the interview. The Chamber does not find, therefore, that D717 sufficiently adds to the evidence already on the record in these proceedings to make it fit for admission. On the basis of the foregoing, the Chamber decides not to admit D717 into evidence and instructs the registrar to change its status in e-court accordingly. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the admission of D717. The next decision to be delivered is a decision on the admission into evidence of two documents, marked for identification P701 and P704. On the 21st of July 2008 during the testimony of witness Alun Roberts, the Prosecution tendered a Globus article from the 11th of August, 1995 as P701, together with an accompanying map as P704, which can be found at transcript page 6815. On the 21st of July, the Gotovina Defence objected to the announced tendering of these documents in paragraph 4 of its response to the Prosecution's submission of Alun Roberts' 92 ter statement and associated exhibits. The Gotovina Defence alleged that the witness did not establish a foundation for the tendering of these items. The article gives detailed information, inter alia, of the Croatian army's advancement in Operation Storm, the five corps and Military Districts involved and their commanders by name, which is further illustrated by the map. These facts are material to the background issues of this case and are therefore relevant. The author of the article mentions Croatian generals as his sources but falls short of naming names. Furthermore, Alun Roberts' witness statement of the 31st of July 1998 corroborates parts of the article with firsthand information that General Gotovina and Colonel Norac were commanders of the Split and Gospic Military Districts respectively. The contemporaneous publication in Globus corroborates by a description of the situation in line with some of Roberts' observations, the statement of the latter. Although the probative value of this publication is very limited, it meets the test of Rule 89 (C). For these reasons the Chamber admits the article and the map. The Chamber requests that the registrar change the status of these documents in e-court accordingly. The next decision to be delivered is -- actually, not a decision but gives further reasons for private session testimony of a portion of Soren Liborius's testimony. Pursuant to Rule 79 (B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Chamber will provide the reasons, in public, for excluding the public from a portion of the testimony of witness Soren Liborius. On the 12th of September, 2008, at transcript page 8543, the witness requested to go into private session when asked to provide further explanation of a statement made in his diary, which is a public document in this case.
