The Chamber, having heard the submissions by the parties on this matter, took a short break to deliberate on the witness's request. The Chamber carefully balanced the need to safeguard the public character of the trial with the interests of justice in hearing evidence from the witness which it anticipated would be of importance to the Chamber in accessing -- assessing the evidence presented in these proceedings. In addition, Soren Liborius was a European Union monitoring mission monitor at the time of the events about which he testified and the Chamber acknowledges that the EUMM is an organisation which has legitimate concerns about the disclosure of personal details of their staff. For these reasons and pursuant to 79(A)(iii), the Chamber decided, in this particular situation, that it was in the interests of justice to allow the witness to answer a number of questions put to him on a question-by-question basis in private session. And this concludes the Chamber's reasons pursuant to 79(B)(iii). The Chamber still owes the parties the reasons for the -- for granting the request for a video-conference link for Witness 52, and these are then the Chamber's reasons for its decision to allow the Prosecution's motion requesting leave to present the evidence of Witness 52 via video-conference link on the 8th of October, 2008 pursuant to Rule 81 bis of the Rules. On the 29th of September 2008, the Prosecution filed a motion requesting leave to present the evidence of Witness 52 via video-conference link from Croatia on the 8th of October 2008. The Defence for Gotovina, Cermak, and Markac, respectively filed responses not objecting to the motion. Having received an informal indication of the Defence position, the Chamber decided, on the 2nd of October, 2008, to grant the motion and informed the parties and the registry accordingly through informal communication. According to Rule 81 bis of the Rules the Chamber may order that proceedings be conducted by way of video-conference link if this is consistent with the interests of justice. As previously set out by this Chamber, the standard of Rule 81 bis is met if a witness is unable to come to the Tribunal, if the testimony is sufficiently important to make it unfair to the requesting party to proceed without it, and if the accused is not prejudiced in his or her right to confront the witness. A medical doctor established that the witness, who is in her mid-80s, was unable, because of her age and her medical condition, to travel to The Hague. Having reviewed the witness's medical certificate provided by the Prosecution, the Chamber found that the witness was unable to travel to The Hague to testify. On the basis of the witness statement which was provided to the Chamber earlier, the Chamber was further satisfied that her testimony would be sufficiently important to make it unfair to the Prosecution to proceed without it. Finally, the parties did not argue and the Chamber did not find that the accused would be prejudiced in the exercise of their right to confront the witness. Consequently, the Chamber found that it was consistent with the interests of justice to grant the Prosecution's request to hear Witness 52's testimony via video-conference link. And the this concludes the reasons for the Chamber's decision. Last decision to be delivered, or should I say the last reasons to be delivered are the reasons for granting trial-related protective measures for Witness 1. On the 2nd of September, 2008, the Prosecution filed a motion requesting that the Chamber order the trial-related protective measures of pseudonym and face distortion for Witness 1. On the 4th of September, 2008, the Markac Defence filed a response, requesting that the Chamber deny the motion. On the 5th of September, 2008, the Cermak Defence filed its response, indicating that while it did not oppose the request for protective measures, it disagreed with the Prosecution's arguments in support of the motion. On the same day, the Gotovina Defence filed its response similarly raising no objections to the request for protective measures but disputing the Prosecution's position that Witness 1's testimony would antagonise individuals inside Croatia. On the 15th of September, 2008, at transcript page 8691, the Chamber granted the protective measures sought for Witness 1, being pseudonym and face distortion. Thereafter, as an almost inevitable consequence, the parties discussed the situation and agreed that the testimony of Witness 1 should be heard in closed session, given the nature of the testimony. That discussion can be found at transcript pages 8696 and 8697. On the same day the Chamber decided to hear the testimony of Witness 1 in closed session. This decision can be found at transcript page 8698. According to Rule 75, a chamber may order appropriate measures for the privacy and protection of witnesses, provided that the measures are consistent with the rights of the accused. The Chamber held in its reasons for its first protective measures decision in this case, which can be found at transcript pages 2610 and 2611, that the party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family, should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. This standard can be satisfied by showing, for example, that a threat was made against the witness or the witness's family. The mere expression of fear by a person is insufficient to justify protective measures. Witness 1 is a Serb who expressed fear for his safety and the safety of his elderly father who remains in Knin. In 2008, Witness 1 returned to Croatia for the first time since 1995. Within a week of his return, Witness 1 was questioned at the police station and in the presence of Croatian police officers regarding the incident about which he testified. Further, during the week preceding his testimony, Witness 1 was visited at his home by two men whom he believed were Croatian police officers. The men questioned Witness 1 about his contact with individuals in The Hague. For the aforementioned reasons, the Chamber found that the Prosecution had demonstrated an objectively grounded risk to the security of Witness 1, should it become known that he has given evidence before the Tribunal. The Chamber considered that, in light of the nature of the anticipated evidence of this witness, granting the protective measures, as requested in the motion, would be insufficient, and therefore the Chamber decided to hear the witness's testimony in closed session. And this concludes the Chamber's reasons for its decision to grant protective measures for Witness 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To have a new number, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A new number. Mr. Registrar, my assumption that it would be D877, is that right? Yes. I -- it's on the record that it is right and it is admitted into evidence. There further is another matter which relates to the report which was introduced through the last witness, not the witness we heard today, where there was some discussion about whether filing was done timely, and when the witness was in court, Mr. Kuzmanovic added one objection to admission of that report, which was about events that have taken place in Sector North and at dates different from the visit by that mission of which of witness was a member. utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was section 6, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.text: Section 6.
